entries.claim: The dotted-path walker cannot distinguish a literal property containing a dot from a nested path, so `unset` can delete a different key than the caller requested.
entries.failure_scenario: Given `{"a.b":"retired","a":{"b":"live"}}`, running `config.mjs unset --file <file> a.b` splits the argument into `["a","b"]`, deletes the live nested `a.b`, and leaves the literal top-level `"a.b"` untouched. Because this command intentionally accepts arbitrary unknown keys, literal dotted properties are valid migration inputs; this path removes more than requested while reporting `removed:["a.b"]`.
entries.counter_evidence: The ambiguity is real but the failing shape is unreachable through any supported path, and the split is not divergent behaviour introduced here. Cadence config layers store NESTED objects: .planning/config.json top-level keys are review, model, git, stakes and it holds no literal dotted key. `setInto(obj, dotted, value)` at config.mjs:321 predates this range (present at 76e2b20f) and splits a dotted argument exactly the same way, as do get and validate, so a literal "a.b" property is unreachable by every read and write face in the file, not only by unset. A config holding one could not be read by `get` or written by `set` either. HIGH overstates it: unset is consistent with its siblings rather than removing more than the rest of the seam would.

entries.claim: Parsing the entire schema-blind layer into JavaScript numbers and serializing it after a removal can corrupt unrelated values that were not requested for deletion.
entries.failure_scenario: Given `{"stakes":"critical","extension":{"id":9007199254740993}}`, unsetting only `stakes` parses the unrelated integer as the rounded Number `9007199254740992`; line 430 then writes that changed value back. The command promises to remove named paths while leaving siblings alone and explicitly accepts unknown data, but an untrusted or extension-owned integer outside the safe range is silently modified.
entries.counter_evidence: Confirmed as a real round-trip hazard, and NOT a regression from this range. At 76e2b20f, before unset existed, config.mjs already did JSON.parse at line 355 and atomicWrite(file, JSON.stringify(cfg, null, 2)) at line 370 in `set` - so every config write in this codebase has always re-serialized the whole layer, and unset inherits that rather than introducing it. The range under review therefore did not create the defect the finding names. Reachability is also narrow: every schema value is an enum, bool, string, array or a small int (the largest is review.request_timeout_ms at 540000), so an unsafe integer requires a hand-written or extension-owned key with no producer in the tree. Recorded as a standing config-write defect rather than a blocker on this range.
